analysis.one_liner: Adds a 10% surtax on income above $1–2 million a year.
analysis.headline: The Millionaires Surtax Act, which would add a 10% tax on income above $1 million to $2 million a year, was introduced with 7 House Democratic cosponsors in June 2021 and never received a hearing or vote in the Ways and Means Committee before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a 10% surtax on each dollar of income above $2 million a year for joint filers and above $1 million for everyone else [S2][S3]. The money would be new federal revenue collected only from the roughly 0.2% of taxpayers with the very highest incomes [S3]. It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee for the entire two-year Congress without a hearing, markup, or floor vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit indirectly: the surtax falls entirely on people earning over $1–2 million a year, and the revenue it raises could reduce what everyone else pays or fund public services without touching middle-income households [S3]. Taxpayers below the threshold pay nothing under the bill [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 10% tax on modified adjusted gross income above $2 million for joint filers and surviving spouses, and above $1 million for all other taxpayers, applied to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021 [S2][S3].

The surtax is in addition to existing income tax, so only the highest-earning filers would pay it; it contains special rules so nonresident aliens and Americans living abroad are taxed on the same base as under current law [S3].
The bill specifically disallows a deduction for investment interest in computing the surtax base, so investment income cannot be sheltered from the surtax through interest deductions [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Individuals with income above $1 million ($2 million for joint returns) would pay the 10% surtax on income above those thresholds. Wealthy households with large investment income lose some ability to deduct investment interest when calculating the surtax base [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill is a pure revenue measure that does not dedicate the money to any specific program, so its benefits to working people depend entirely on how Congress later chooses to spend the revenue [S3].

The surtax applies to income, not wealth, so it does not address unrealized capital gains — a billionaire whose wealth grows through untaxed appreciation would owe nothing on those gains until they are sold [S3].

A 10% surtax on top of federal, and in high-tax states state, rates raises top marginal rates noticeably, which critics argue discourages work and investment at the top; supporters counter that it applies only to income above the thresholds [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct cost falls on a small group of very high earners, and the revenue would be real. But the bill never advanced, and even if it had, it is a narrow tax on reported income rather than a broader reform; its benefit to ordinary people is real but indirect, depending on future spending decisions.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced in June 2021 and stayed there — with no hearing, markup, or floor vote — until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Don Beyer introduced the Millionaires Surtax Act on June 11, 2021, with six Democratic colleagues as original cosponsors (Mr. Cohen, Mr. Lowenthal, Mr. Panetta, Mr. Blumenauer, Ms. Schakowsky, and Ms. Lofgren) [S3][S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, which is the committee with jurisdiction over income tax rates [S1][S5].
Seven Democratic representatives cosponsored the bill in total, and no Republican cosponsors are listed [S4].

The complete action history shows only two actions: introduction and referral to committee. No further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died in committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households earning over $1–2 million a year are better off because the bill never advanced — they avoid the 10% surtax. No committee process ever occurred, so no industry or interest group needed to campaign against it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners, untouched by the surtax

for.name: Rep. Don Beyer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Millionaires Surtax Act and drafted it to impose a 10% surtax on income above $1–2 million [S3].

for.name: 6 of 224 House Democrats
for.role: Original cosponsors (Reps. Cohen, Lowenthal, Panetta, Blumenauer, Schakowsky, and Lofgren)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original cosponsors at introduction [S3][S4].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral on June 11, 2021 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died in committee at the end of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 7 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republicans cosponsored; the bill never advanced far enough for a roll-call vote [S4].

industries.note: The bill's only direct payers: individuals above the $1 million / $2 million joint-filer thresholds would pay a 10% surtax on income above those levels [S3]. Keeping the bill in committee preserved the status quo for these households [S5].

industries.industry: Tax-advantaged investment strategies (leverage and interest deduction planning)
industries.note: The surtax base specifically reduces adjusted gross income by investment-interest deductions, limiting the ability to shield investment income with borrowed-money interest costs [S3].
